title: This school for clairvoyants knows just how to affirm your powers
excerpt: 'It's like Hogwarts, only better because it's real' says director Rani August of the Berkeley Psychic institute
content:
When Rani August first walked into the Berkeley Psychic Institute (BPI) in 2008, the downpour outside gave her arrival the Stygian feel of Suspiria‘s opening scene: a stranger at the rain-drenched threshold of an unfamiliar world. For August, though, the other side of the doorway promised belonging.

Inside, she heard people openly talking about things she had kept private for decades, like seeing energy, communicating with spirits, and practicing healing. She remembers getting chills and tearing up as she realized she had finally found what she had been searching for all her life.

“It felt like coming home,” August tells 48 Hills. “Coming to BPI was like going to Hogwarts, only better because it was real!”

Today, the institute she describes as her spiritual home is also where she works. The Rev. Rani August has served as director of Berkeley Psychic Institute since 2021, overseeing classes, teachers, staff, and the Clairvoyant Training Program while teaching and offering professional readings and healings.

Her approach centers on helping people develop what she considers their innate psychic abilities. That mission began with a childhood sense of difference.

August says her earliest psychic memories date to around age three, when she saw auras and spirits and communicated with a spirit guide. At first, she assumed everyone experienced the world the same way.

Certainly not her mother, who witnessed one of these mystifying conversations in her daughter’s bedroom, in what must have looked like a horrifying scene from Hide and Seek. August recalls asking questions, listening, and responding to someone her mother could neither see nor hear. 

August says another detail made the encounter especially puzzling: the conversation was in French, a language she had not yet encountered.

“Experiences like that taught me to pay attention to people’s reactions and to keep most of what I saw to myself,” she says.

At BPI, she was finally able to explore her power. August enrolled in Meditation 1, the introductory course that remains the foundation of the institute’s training.

In an early class, a teacher asked students to make a “mock-up,” a visualization meant to help them create something they wanted. August pictured winning a raffle for a free psychic reading. Minutes later, she says, her name was called.

For August, the moment encouraged trust in perceptions she had previously doubted and opened a playful question: What else might she learn?

She graduated as valedictorian of the Clairvoyant Program in 2010 and went on to pursue advanced programs in teaching, ministry, healing, and trance mediumship. But she describes the most consequential changes in everyday terms: boundaries, relationships, and relief from feeling overwhelmed.

August had always thought of herself as an introvert. She loved being around people, but often found it exhausting. Through her training, she realized she was taking on other people’s energy. 

Learning to separate their experiences from her own changed the way she helped others. “I could care deeply without carrying what they were carrying,” she says. “I could have boundaries and still be loving.”

The lesson now informs her classroom. In Meditation 1, students sit in chairs with their feet on the ground and their eyes closed, practicing what BPI calls psychic tools. They learn grounding, releasing unwanted energy, and calling their own energy back—with questions and laughter accompanying the exercises.

“One of the first things we validate is that everyone is psychic,” she says. “You don’t come to BPI to become psychic. You are already psychic!”

For beginners, that invitation can feel intimidating. Allison Thompson remembers feeling nervous and scared before her first class, then finding reassurance in August’s openheartedness.

“Her teaching style was always warm, welcoming, and light-hearted for a subject that can feel scary to many people,” says Thompson.

She subsequently took five classes with August and completed the beginner series.

Further training requires substantial commitment. Clairvoyant Program student Danielle McQueen describes a one- to two-year course, with requirements often totaling 20 hours a week.

“She has high standards and operates a rigorous program with care and kindness,” McQueen says of August. “She wants you to succeed and to get the most out of your time at BPI.”

In readings, August describes clairvoyance as visual information appearing through colors, textures, images, words, and symbols. She says she needs no personal history beforehand. 

Student readings follow a format involving visual symbols, the aura, and chakras. Her professional sessions are less structured and begin with whatever draws her attention in a person’s aura.

A reading communicates what she says she sees; healing, as BPI defines it, involves changing energy. Her professional readings include healing; student readings do not.

“The person receiving the healing is always in charge of their own space,” says August. “They get to choose what they are ready to change or release, and the healing honors where they are in that moment.”

Author, coach, and educator Amrita Rose wrote following a session that she was inspired to enroll in Meditation 1.

“I continue to experience a shift in my energy and space,” Rose remarked.

For August, the work has also challenged habits developed during years in public education and academia. An analytical approach that once served her could, she found, interfere with what she experienced as clairvoyance.

“I had to learn to stop trying so hard, let go of needing to figure everything out, and allow myself to be present and see what is there,” she says.

That shift carries into leadership. Scheduling classes means checking teachers’ availability and finding suitable times, but August says she also considers which teachers, classes, and combinations appear to fit energetically. She gathers practical information, speaks with colleagues, and consults senior leadership when appropriate.

“My clairvoyance isn’t separate from my leadership,” says August. “It is at the center of how I lead.”

In her sessions, an immediate question can lead to a deeper conversation. August recalls a woman asking whether an ex-partner would return. She says the reading led instead to a childhood experience of abandonment and the client’s recognition of how it shaped later relationships.

For August, the encounter showed how looking beneath a question could reveal a pattern someone was ready to change.

Student Erika Young went through a similar journey of discovery. She came in with questions she had not quite figured out how to ask, and during her first session with August, she found tools that helped her feel more grounded. Later, well into the Clairvoyant Program, she said she understood herself better than ever.

August also talks about knowing when to keep something to yourself, a practice BPI calls “psychic manners.” Before sharing what you see, she says, consider whether the person wants to know—and respect their boundaries. Just because you pick up on something does not mean you have to say it.

She welcomes skeptics to ask questions and try the tools themselves. In her view, the future is open, not predetermined, like a Final Destination premise.

“A psychic reading gives you information, and you decide what to do with it,” August says. “You remain the creator of your own life.”

For August, who learned as a child to hide what she saw, teaching now means giving others room to ask questions, experiment, and find their own answers.
